utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning everyone. The Chamber will be sitting this week in the absence of Judge Nosworthy who is on other authorised trial business in connection with the trial of Martic. Now, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The Prosecution would like to make an application for witness protection measures for an upcoming witness. At some point I would suggest that maybe we could deal with that as the first thing this morning. If Your Honours agree with that, then I would request that we go into private session for a brief moment while we deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is an application that was intimated on the 19th of September. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, we notified the Defence on the 19th of September that we considered making an application at that point in time. We thought -- we had hoped we could make the application in writing, but we did not feel we had the facts sufficiently clear to be able to make a written application and we had only got the last information in for the application yesterday afternoon. So that is why I am on my feet now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, can you tell me what the Defence position is in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We have some concerns about this application, in particular the -- whether or not the case is made out to justify the measures requested. And if -- and if the Chamber feels that they are made out, we do have an additional objection to the keeping of this log-book that the Prosecution is requesting from us. We find that a bit onerous that we have to keep a log of any disclosure of this person's identity for the purposes of investigation and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall hear what Mr. Marcussen has to say in supplement to the e-mail that was sent to the Trial Chamber, which you presumably have a copy of. And just give me a moment before we embark on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Marcussen, we're satisfied that in view of the issues that are raised by this application, namely the risk to the security of the witness, it is appropriate to hear the application in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are satisfied that the objective test for the granting of protective measures is satisfied in this case, particularly with reference to the likely content of the witness's evidence when taken in association with the various points made by the Prosecution about the witness's basis for his fear, these points also being set out in the e-mail intimating the application. So the witness will be referred to by the pseudonym K83 and will give evidence by voice -- with voice and image distortion. The other measures sought will also be granted and reflected in a written decision. We are reserve our decision on the question of the log to compare the circumstances here with the circumstances in the other cases in which we have required that a log be kept. Only then can we make a final decision on whether this case can be regarded as of such an exceptional nature as to warrant that further measure, but we'll make an announcement of our decision on that in the course of today. Now, that completes the application. We now proceed with the next witness, I take it, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Hamide Fondaj. Ms. Fondaj is a Rule 92 bis (B) -- or what was formerly known as Rule 92 bis (B). I take it now she should be referred to as Rule 92 ter. And the paragraphs to which she refers to in the indictment or that are relevant to her evidence are paragraphs 72(b) [sic], 73, and 77 of the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say (b) or (d)?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 72(b). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No -- oh, I'm sorry. Yes, 72(d). She's a Suva Reka witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, so it should be (d) in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see the transcript is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 73 and 77. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would like to formally introduce Ms. Nadia Zed to the Chamber. I have provided the required letters to you this morning and she will be participating today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. As you know, the Chamber will recognise Ms. Zed in the course of this week. There is probably one other outstanding document, and Mr. Boas will speak to you about that sometime in the course of the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Fondaj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you should know that we already have before us your statement, so we know what it is you will be telling us about, we've read it, we have that information already. The purpose of the questions you will be asked is to clarify things or perhaps to explain some of it more fully and also to enable counsel for the accused to challenge certain things that they may wish to challenge in your evidence. The important thing is to fix your mind on the particular question you're asked and try to concentrate your answer on the point that is raised with you in the question. The first person to question you then will be for the Prosecution, Ms. Kravetz. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please state your name, for the record.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Hamide Fondaj, from the village of Peqan in the municipality of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just answered my second question actually. Mrs. Fondaj, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution on 9th June 2001 concerning events that you experienced or witnessed in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had the chance to review your statement, Mrs. Fondaj?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In the course of this review of your statement, are you satisfied that the contents of this statement accurately reflect to the best of your knowledge and recollection the truth about the events that are described in the statement?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to tender this witness's statement as Exhibit P02283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, on page 3 of your statement you describe how on 21st March you and your family had to leave your village of Peqan because it came under attack of Serb forces. Can you tell us where did you go from your village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: On the 21st of March, from the village of Peqan, I went to the village of Nishor. I stayed there for a week. During that week, we were shelled also at Nishor, so from Nishor - because we could not stay there anymore --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, I'm going to stop you there. Can I ask you in the interests of saving time that you pay close attention to the questions I ask and only respond to the specific question I'm asking. Thank you. You said the village of Peqan was attacked on 21st of March. At the time of the attack was there any KLA presence in the village of Peqan?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where exactly in the village was the KLA based?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: In the village of Peqan, in our village it was a shop where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And approximately how many members of the KLA were based in Peqan at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how many of them there were, but I know that there were some.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. At this time, was anyone in your family with the KLA, a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was he with you on the day of the attack of -- against Peqan?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. He was with the KLA, with the people that were with the KLA. I was alone at home with my children, two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you said that from Peqan you went to the village of Nishor and you remained there for one week?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you later have to leave the village of Nishor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I had to leave. We spent a whole night in Kasterca village close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why did you have to leave the village of -- why did you have to leave the village of Nishor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Because of the bombing from the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you left Nishor, did you leave alone with your family or did other inhabitants of the village of Nishor also leave on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. All the inhabitants left, inhabitants from the municipality of Suhareke, the villages, we all left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you spent a night in the village of Kasterca? Is that correct? My pronunciation is probably not correct. And where did you continue from there?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We stayed the whole day in the mountains. At night we left the mountain and we went in the direction of Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Fondaj, why did you head specifically in the direction of Belanica? Why didn't you go to another village or back to Peqan?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: There was nowhere else to go. Every other route was blocked. That was the only route we could take.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you were travelling at this time alone with your family or with other people from the village of Nishor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: All the families were there from Nishor, Doberdolan, Samadrexha. There were thousands of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So when you arrived in Belanica, approximately how many people do you estimate had gathered there?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know how many. There were thousands and thousands of people. You -- there was no place to throw a cat; that's how I could explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where exactly did you stay in the village of Belanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I stayed with family, their surname is Kapexholi. It was close to the corridor in Bellanice, in the middle of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And approximately how many people were you in this house with this family?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We were about 50 or 60 people in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Fondaj, on page 3 of your statement you state that on 1st April, 1999, Serb forces began firing at houses in Belanica. Were you able to see this firing yourself?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Because it -- the bullets flew above our heads, above our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And from which direction was the firing coming, originating?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: At the edge of Bellanice. So from the edge of Bellanice, the firing came towards us, above our heads, above the houses. And all the tiles of the roof fell down because of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At the time this attack against Belanica started, were you -- were you aware of -- if there was any KLA presence in the village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was there any outgoing fire from Belanica towards these Serb positions from where they were firing?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you do, Mrs. Fondaj, when you realised that this was happening, when you realised that they were shooting in the direction of the house where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: All of us gathered in a basement of that house, and we stayed for about two hours there, the 50 or 60 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you later decide to leave the house where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. We decided to go -- to go to the centre of the village, and we decided to go there and stand there, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you got to the centre of the village, had other people also gathered there or was it just this group of 50 or 60 people?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, the whole population was there. Everybody was sitting and standing so tight, very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We stayed there for about half an hour, and we heard from people that everybody had to get on their tractors and stay there, where we were. We went into the courtyard and we got on the tractors. We were frightened that if we were at home, they would come and get us at home and a massacre would happen. So that's why all of us decided to go to the centre of the village, the whole population, so that we would be together there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you heard from people that you had to gather there and take your tractors. From whom did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Well, word after word people were saying that we had to get on our tractors and be there all together, but everybody had to be on their tractors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While you were there in this -- in the centre of town, in this clearing, did -- at any time did these forces that were shelling this city -- the town, did you see them enter the village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: When we were at the house where we were staying -- when we got on the tractors, there were people in masks that came from tractor to tractor. Then they came to our tractor and they asked us to give them a hundred marks, each of us, because if we wouldn't give them a hundred marks they would kill us. So they went from tractor to tractor doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Fondaj, you said you saw people in masks going from tractor to tractor. Can you describe anything else about these people, what sort of uniform they were wearing, if they were wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: The first that came had masks on, black masks on, and you could see only their eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How were they dressed, these people that approached your tractor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Black.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For -- you said you stayed there for several hours. Did you at some point leave that area, this clearing where you were in your tractor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. We went into a street, and we stayed the whole night there. It was raining.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While you spent the night there outdoors, did anyone else approach your tractor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: That night it was dark and the whole night nobody came until the morning. We stayed on the tractors in the rain, outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The following morning, were you able to leave the village of Belanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. The next day there was another offensive. They came to our tractors, the policemen. They had bandannas and painted faces, all kinds of uniforms came to our village -- to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you saw men in different types of uniforms in the village, and what happened when these men approached your tractor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Before they came to us, there were three elderly men who went up to them and asked them: What do you intend to do with the population? And they said: Everybody get on their tractors and put a white sign on the tractor. Those who don't have this white sign will be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This happened on the second day of the offensive, what you're now describing?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, the next day, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, you spent the next day in Belanica? This is the two --

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, we stayed until the forces came because it was impossible to get out. Everybody was on their tractors. So they came from tractor to tractor until our turn came, my tractor's turn came. It was about 10.00. When they came to us, we had two elderly men on the tractor. They asked money from them. These two elderly men gave them each a hundred marks, and they beat them up because they didn't want just a hundred marks from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say they came and they beat them up. Who are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: They were uniformed, all kinds of uniforms were there in Bellanice. Some of them had black uniforms and masks. There were policemen. There were people who were naked and had painted bodies. They had knives in their hands and threatened us to slit our necks. All kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you eventually able to leave the town -- the village of Belanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: So after they beat up those two elderly men, they came to me. They pointed the automatic rifle at me and asked: Do you like NATO? I didn't say anything. Do you like Clinton? Do you like Rugova? Where is the KLA? Why are they not protecting you? Where is your husband? But I did not answer. My daughter was on the tractor with me and she was really frightened. At that time she stepped on my foot and told me: Mom, give them the money because they will kill us. And they still had the automatic gun on me, showing to me that they would kill me if I did not give them the money, so I gave them the money. And they went from tractor to tractor doing the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, I understand what you have just described is in your statement, and I understand they went from tractor to tractor collecting this money. You at some point, according to your statement, headed out of Belanica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: When we went to the end of the village of Bellanice, which is only about 1 kilometre away, we were stopped about ten times and we gave about 10.000 marks. We were, as I said, stopped and asked for money. We were offended. They said all kinds of things to us, but this happened until we got out of Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you left Belanica, in which direction did you head?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We left Bellanice and we wanted to go in the direction of Suhareke. We came across an army convoy, and they told us not to go in the direction of Suhareke but in the direction of Rahovec, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, on page 4 of your statement you describe how at some point while you were travelling you passed the village -- the town of Malisevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you arrived to Malisevo you state in your written statement that your tractor broke down and that someone ordered you to continue or you would be placed behind a barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Our tractor broke down, it wouldn't start, so somebody wanted to tow us, but they came and told us: If your tractor won't go, then you have to come beyond this barbed wire. There were women and men -- and old men there and children. But our tractor started and we were towed by another tractor. So we went along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, you say there were women and children behind the barbed wire. Where exactly were these women and children?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: There was in Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But where was this barbed wire? Was this a barbed wire along the side of the road or was this on a side of a building?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what it was. It was a school or some kind of building. It was surrounded and circled by barbed wire. And these people were staying there. They were told I think that buses would come and take them to the border, but we don't know what happened. We did not see them anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How many people did you see approximately there? You said "many people." Are you talking about hundreds, thousands of people?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Thousands, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, you continued past Malisevo and did you eventually get to the border?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I would like to say that before we went to Malisheve we were forced to step on the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I have to interrupt you here. As you know, the statement is already in evidence. I'm just asking whether you made it across the border into Albania.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. We went through Krusha e Madhe, Prizren. When we went close to Vermica, we stayed there for one day and one night. The military forces were around the area and they hit my son with a wrench --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm again going to have to stop you. Just one last question. As you were travelling to the border, did you again see any military or police forces on the road?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you see them just occasionally or did you see them frequently along the road?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. The whole way when we got -- until we got to the border, these military forces were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the order will be: General Lazarevic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Ojdanic, General Lukic, and General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Fondaj. I name Djuro Cepic, one of the Defence counsel on the team of Vladimir Lazarevic. I would like to put a few questions to you. I'll do my best to make them concise and clear, so I am asking you for clear and concise answers, if possible, and the best thing would be for you to give me yes or no answers. Thank you. Mrs. Fondaj, in your statement you said that up to the 21st of March, 1999, you were in the village of Pecane, that for the most part all villagers had left the village, or most of them?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That you used bunkers in front of the house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That bunker was made by your husband with his colleagues from the KLA, right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. It was myself and my children that built that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you. You come to the village of Belanica. You probably know that the KLA headquarters in the village of Belanica was in the school, right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. There weren't any KLA. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, you said that your husband left you a uniform and some pictures. Did he leave that on that morning when the Serb police entered the village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. He left them at home, but I took them along. I took them in order for the clothes to be sent to him, but for ten days I did not see my husband so I couldn't give them to my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And did he continue to move about in civilian clothing, since he had left his uniform behind. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. He had a uniform, but he was not there and I took this uniform and I was with the other part of the population. I followed the rest of the citizens, where they went when we were on the tractors. I went to Albania. I did not see him anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understand you, Mrs. Fondaj, but what was your husband wearing when he left you? Was he wearing civilian clothing. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: My husband did not leave me, but he joined the KLA. I don't know where he was, where they went. But the uniform he left at home I took with me, so that probably he would come and meet us and he wanted to change his uniform, so that's why I kept it. But my husband was not with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You told us that you did not see your husband for ten days. Can you tell us the date when the ten days began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My husband joined from the time the -- he joined the KLA in the village and he was not with me all that time. I was alone at home with my two children, and I left with the rest of the villagers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question was very specific. You said you did not see him for ten days. Can you tell me, please, when the ten days began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 21st when we left, I did not see him for the week I stayed in Nishor. I stayed in Bellanice for three or four days, and I did not see him for the whole period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, when you last saw him on the 21st, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A KLA uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude, then, that he had two KLA uniforms. Is that right? One that he wore and the other one that he left you?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, he had a uniform, another one. He had underwear that was available for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in the village of Belanica in the convoy in which you left the village there were mainly elderly men. Were all the younger men with the KLA in the hills? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know where the men were. Where I was, there were children, elderly people. I didn't see many young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Further on you say in your statement that you were moving along in a convoy by Ostrozub and you see that houses are burned there. Those who were by Ostrozub had uniforms on. Were they people between the ages of 30 and 40?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see what -- of what age they were. There were policemen, there were people wearing military uniforms, those that burned the houses in Ostrozub while we were passing through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Due to the distance involved, you could not see any insignia on these military uniforms, right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, they were close. We were moving along the road, and there was army on both sides of the road. And we could see them in groups, in different houses, 15 or 20 in one group torching one house, and another group torching another. Ostrozub is a big village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. They had bandannas on their heads, right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, no. Not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you couldn't see any insignia on their shoulders, right? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see the insignia, no. I didn't have time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Fondaj. Thank you, Mrs. Fondaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Fondaj, I'm Toma Fila, attorney-at-law, and I'm going to put some brief questions to you regarding these uniforms. I don't find this very clear. You said that you saw your husband on the 21st of April, and that he left in a uniform, if I understood you correctly. And then you spent seven days in one village and then three days in another village and then you crossed the border. Could you please tell me, if you remember, when it was you saw your husband again? The 25th of April, and what was the next time?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I saw my husband on the 21st of March when I left the village, and I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: So on the 21st of March when I left the village and went to the other village where I spent a week, that's when I saw him last.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And afterwards, when did you next see him? I was the one who misspoke, yes, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: When I returned from Albania, in June or July, that's when I returned to Kosovo, that's when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now we've clarified that. So it's not ten days, it's two months rather. Now, why did he leave his uniform at home? The 21st of March when he left, why did he leave his uniform at home?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: On the 21st of March, he did not leave. He was there with his KLA ranks, but I fled because the village was bombed. And I took my husband's uniform with me. And in Bellanice, out of fear that they might find this uniform, I hid it. And then I crossed the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understood all of that. I'm not challenging that, but why did he leave this other uniform with you at home? Why didn't he take it along? Did you understand me? I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: He was in the village on the 21st with the KLA. Let's say he would spend the day there with the KLA, and in the evening he would come in the house and that's where his uniform was. The uniform was in his house because in the evening he would come to his family, to his children. And then again in the morning, he would go to the KLA in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And he left his uniform at home?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because he would come back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. All right. All right. I have this other question, too. You said that before you arrived at the border you threw away all your personal belongings like books and food supplies that were marked "USA." That is what you stated, right? What kind of food is, this marked USA? I never heard of such food. I saw bombs marked "USA," but not food. That's what they threw all over Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We had flour, cooking oil during the first offensive, and then during the break between the two offensives they brought us these food supplies as aid. We had pastas, flour, and then we had to leave everything behind because we couldn't take everything with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question is who it was that brought this to you. Between two Serb offensives, who brought you this pasta marked "USA"?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: The aid that we received in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a villager who was distributing this food, and I don't know who brought that food to the village. There was a person from my village who was distributing it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, could you repeat that question, please. It was not heard by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is the question: Was this aid given to you by Serbs, this aid marked "USA," or was this aid given to you by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Neither by the Serbs nor by the KLA. It was a humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But this was at the time of the Serb offensives. What kind of humanitarian aid was being distributed then, by who, in that period? This is the period of the bombing, you know.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: In 1998, 1998, during the first offensive we received this humanitarian aid too, and in 1999 when we left the village, then we took these food supplies with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, had you said "1998" immediately, I wouldn't have even asked you anything. I thought you were talking about 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do have some questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Fondaj. My name is Dan Ivetic, and I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic, along with my colleagues, Mr. Branko Lukic and Mr. Ozren Ogrizovic here today. And I'm going to have to ask you some questions relative to the testimony you've just given and the statement that we have received from the Prosecutor regarding what you have stated in that statement. And I would ask you merely to pay close attention to what I ask and to try and give me the most truthful and concise answer possible since our time here is limited and we have a number of things we need to cover. Now, my first question will deal with your husband. In your statement you say that he was part of a police independent union. I want to ask you first: Was he armed during the time-period that he was in this union?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, he was not armed. He used to be a policeman but he stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have that --

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, this police independent union, this was a parallel structure set up by the Kosovo Albanian political leaders in the area to replace the state institutions of the Republic of Serbia as part of their pro-independence movement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that he was part of this union. He would go to distribute aid to other people because people were in need of supplies. We were given humanitarian aid by the Red Cross, by Mother Teresa, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... heard about the humanitarian aid you've received. I have some other areas I want to question you about. Now, is it correct that members of the independent police union such as your husband, that most of them became armed fighters within the structure of the so-called UCK/KLA sometime in 1998?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know about others, but my husband joined the KLA because he was a former prisoner as well and he saw it necessary to join the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: For others, I don't know. My husband joined the KLA in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am. Well, what about in your home village of Pecane. In addition to your husband do you know of any other persons, are there any other men who joined the UCK/KLA from your home village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: In Peqan, everybody had a member of the family who was a KLA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would it be fair to say, ma'am, just as you have stated in your statement that there were active KLA fighters in the village in 1998, would it be also accurate to state that throughout the first few months of 1999 there was a constant presence of KLA fighters located in your home village of Pecane?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: In 1998 up to August, that's when the offensive took place, the village was burned and nobody was in the village. Yes, I understand, but I want to link it up with the period of 1999, early 1999. When we returned, the KLA reorganised itself in Peqan village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And again, my question was for the first -- for January and February and most of March of 1999, was the KLA constantly present in your home village of Pecane?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. During these months, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And would it also be accurate to state that the UCK/KLA also had a constant and numerous presence in the other surrounding villages in your municipality of Suva Reka, both throughout 1998 and the first three months of 1999? Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know for other villages, but I have seen them in my village. And in my statement I've stated things that I've seen myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the surrounding areas, were there Serbian police check-points on the roadways, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Not in Peqan roads. There were in Suhareke, Biraq, and Shiroka.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you through our own knowledge or through our husband know of any attacks performed by the KLA upon these check-points?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know. I was in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And is it correct that the KLA forces in the area engaged in frequent armed battles with the Serb forces, both in 1998 and the first three months of 1999 in the Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. Not in Peqan. There were no armed battles in Peqan. They bombed the village. They entered it with the forces, and we had to leave, to flee to other villages. In Semetisht there were armed clashes, but we were in Nishor for five, six days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll get to your departure from your home village a little bit later. I'd like to finish up with some other questions first, dealing again with the period of 1998 and the first three months of 1999. And for that period, ma'am, is it correct or did you have knowledge of the KLA engaging in any acts of kidnapping of civilians, both ethnic Albanian and ethnic Serb, in the Suva Reka region or municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stated your husband would return to spend time with his family with the evenings. When your husband would return to be with his family, was he still armed? Did he still have his weapons with him?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, he had a weapon with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And during the time-period that he spent with his family, was your husband still wearing his uniform or was he clothed in civilian garb?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: He would not stay in the house for a long time. He would just eat something and go. But he was dressed in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have knowledge of or -- either again personally or through your husband, did you have knowledge of either your husband or other KLA fighters, who in order to stay alive and fool the Serb forces would change their uniforms into civilian gear, so as not to be recognised as fighters. Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of it or seen it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can focus to the period of time in March of 1999, and I believe in your statement you have identified the fact that your husband came to take you from your home village of Pecane to Nishor. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate. My husband was in Peqan when the bombing started. Then he took me to Nishor and returned himself to Peqan. And from that moment, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me ask you a little bit more about when he came to Pecane to take you to Nishor. Is it true that during that same time-period he also ordered or took other people from the village, that is other villagers and told them to flee to Nishor and to other areas?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. I was alone throughout the night in the village. The other villagers had already left with tractors, so when he came I had no way how to go to Nishor myself and he took me there and then went back to Peqan himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's ask -- let's focus on these other villagers that you said had left previously. Isn't it true that they left based upon the directions or orders of the UCK/KLA that were in the village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We didn't wait for a KLA order, because when the bombing started there was no other way out for us. We had to go to a village where there was no bombing going on. There was no need for the KLA to go to every door and tell them to leave. Every head of the family prepared his own family on the tractors and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the KLA in fact tell people to leave your village at any point in time prior to that day, as part of their battle strategy or tactics?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, no. As I said, up to the last moment I was alone in the house. I had nobody to go with. I remained in the house, cared, and waited for my husband to come and fetch me. The other villagers had left because of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if I can ask you about the time-period leading up to when you left Pecane. At any point in time prior to then, did the KLA forces in your village fire upon the Serb forces that were outside of the village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. Because had they fired once, they would have encircled us immediately and they would have done whatever they liked with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, we have talked about your husband on several occasions here today but we have not mentioned his true role within the KLA. Ms. Fondaj, isn't it correct that in March of 1999 your husband was a commanding officer of an entire company of fighters within the 2nd Battalion of the 123rd Brigade of the UCK/KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't ask him what his function was. I know that he was a KLA member. I didn't ask; he didn't tell me anything about his role in the KLA. What I know is that he was a KLA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, did you know that he was stationed and responsible for the KLA forces in your village and in the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't know this. I never asked, as I said, and he never told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you find out at some point in time, perhaps when you came back to Kosovo-Metohija, that your husband had become an even higher-ranking officer at the brigade level of the UCK/KLA in the Suva Reka municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know things that you're mentioning. As I said, I never asked him about his role in the KLA or what he did, what was his function in the KLA. What I know is that he was a KLA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have occasion to see other KLA members coming to him for orders?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't. As I said, my husband would come in the house to check on us, to have something to eat, then he would return to that place where they were stationed. I was not interested in his things. I had my own housework to do and children to look after. But in the house, I've never seen this happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be a good time for a pause? I'm about a little more than halfway through with my cross at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Ms. Fondaj, we will break now for half an hour. Would you just leave the courtroom, please, and we'll see you again at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The court will now adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Fondaj, before the break you testified that every household in your village had someone in the UCK/KLA. Now, I want to ask you: How many households were there total in your village as of March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Two or 300 houses. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know or have any knowledge that your husband's KLA battalion had approximately 500 armed members? Does that figure sound accurate?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mrs. Fondaj, I put it to you that at some point in time prior to your departure from the village of Pecane that someone from the KLA told the villagers to leave the village as part of the KLA's battle plan in the region. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mrs. Fondaj, your husband, Ylmet Fondaj, he gave a sworn statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, just as you have, relative to his knowledge of what occurred in your home village and in the Suva Reka municipality. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would ask the court personnel to put up Exhibit 6D76 on the e-court, the excerpt of the English statement of Ylmet Fondaj. We do not have a copy in Albanian, as the Office of the Prosecutor has not, to my knowledge, disclosed this particular statement to us in the Albanian language, but I will limit my examination of the witness from this document just to the two items that are excerpted and hopefully my reading of these statements will be translated to the witness so that she can comment upon the sworn testimony of her husband. If we could turn to the second page on e-court, and the excerpted material there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, ma'am, this statement, dated the 28th of August, 2001, is for an Ylmet, Y-l-m-e-t, Fondaj, father's first name Selim and date of birth of March 28th, 1957 in Pecane, Suva Reka municipality. Is that biographical information that of your husband, Ylmet?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as I've stated, I do not have a copy of the statement in Albanian, so I'm going to read for you the excerpted material in that statement and ask if it refreshes your recollection. Now, first of all, on the first page, it says: "I was married 1978 and we got three children, two sons and one daughter. After my release from prison, I worked with my brother as a house builder in order to survive. In order to feel safe for my family and myself, I joined the KLA in February 1998 and served with the forces to the end of the war. I was commander for a company in the Brigade 123 in the beginning. Later on I advanced as an officer called S2 in the brigade level." Now, ma'am, does this refresh your recollection as to the position that your husband held within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I did not ask my husband what position he had in the KLA. I saw he had a KLA uniform, but as I said I did not ask him what his role was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to sit closer to the microphone for the interpreter's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, ma'am. And again if you could try to make sure to speak into the microphones so that the interpreters can record accurately everything you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would ask for the next page of the exhibit in e-court to be put up on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while that's happening, ma'am, I would like to ask you: As far as the tactics and activities of the KLA, based upon what you have told us, your husband would know better than you what those tactics and actions undertaken were, would he not?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Of course he should know, he should have known better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to again read the portion that is excerpted from your husband's statement in English so that you can receive the translation, and then I'll have a question or two relating to that. Now, in -- at page 4 of his statement, which is the second page of the e-court exhibit and the paragraph that is excerpted there, it states: "I will tell that during the second offensive we, the KLA, changed tactic. We told the villagers to flee and we remained in our positions in the villages, in basements and trenches, and met the Serb ground forces when they entered the village. We met them with resistance. Many time the Serb forces had to withdraw. I will mention that the tactic was successful in the village of Pecane." Now, Mrs. Fondaj, does this refresh your recollection as to whether or not your departure from Pecane in March of 1999 and that of your fellow villagers was the direct result of a tactical order or instruction given by your husband as the KLA commander assigned to the area so that he and his fighters could do battle with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Nobody gave me an order. As I told you, the villagers left in the evening because of the shelling by the forces. So they left and I was alone with my children. And when my husband saw that, all the villagers had left, he came and took me to the rest of the villagers. As I said, I did not receive any order myself. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, your husband's statement here seems to imply that this was a tactic utilised by the KLA to tell people to leave and that this tactic was successful in the village of Pecane. Are you trying to tell us that the incidents that his statement talks about here do not relate to your departure from Pecane in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I'm telling the truth here. I don't know about any orders to leave the village. I don't know what they discussed amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- just to be sure that we're talking about the same incident, I will continue with your husband's sworn words that are at the end of this page and going on to the next. It's the last half a sentence on this page and then the next page in e-court, for the usher's information. And I quote: "After the shelling, the ground forces tried to enter the village, but we defended the village during two days. After two days the Serbs reinforced with tanks and heavy weapons and we had to move to another positions in the village of Semetisht. In that village we managed to resist for eight days. It happened on 25th March 1999 until 6th April 1999." And now, ma'am, does this appear to be the precise time-period and the precise events that you have testified here today when you and the remaining villagers from Pecane left that village?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: When do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: March and April of 1999, the end of March and the beginning of April 1999.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: On the 21st of March, I left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you recognise your husband's signature?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention to the screen in front of you. You should have on the left side a signature and then on the right side two signatures. Do you recognise any of these signatures as being that of your husband?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, one of them is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right, ma'am. Now, you don't know of any reason why your husband would lie about the reason that people left his home village of Pecane, do you?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. He's not lying. But from the 21st I was in Nishor. What the army did, how they fought, and everything else, how could I know about those things? We were somewhere else. I don't know what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that your husband and the other members of the KLA gave orders to the other villagers in Pecane, the other 200 to 300 households without your knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: It is possible, but nobody gave me an order. It was my husband who came and took me at home. The others left, as I told you, but I don't know whether it was because of an order or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can focus on the time-period after you left your village and when you were in Nishor. According to your statement - and now we have corroborative information from your husband's statement - it would appear that the KLA engaged in battle with the Serbian forces for a period of eight days. Now, what I want to know is, first of all: How constant was the fighting during that eight-day time-period?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I told you that I was not in Semetisht. I was in another village during that time. In Nishor we could hear the shelling, and we were shelled in Nishor time after time, but I don't know what was happening elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe my question talked about the time-period when you were in Nishor. During that eight-day time-period, how constant or frequent was the fighting between the KLA and the Serbian forces, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you can get an answer to that question, Mr. Ivetic, you'll have to have a foundation for her knowledge of the fighting by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think she's in fact answered that, but I can ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: She mentioned that she was -- about -- just one moment. I believe in the statement, Your Honour, that's been admitted into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says: "I stayed in Nishor for one week, during which time there was continual shelling going on. Because of the resistance of the KLA from the village of Semetisht where they were deployed, the Serb army was not able to enter Nishor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That does provide a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, I would again ask you the question that I asked. During the time-period you were in Nishor, how constant or frequent was the fighting between the KLA and the Serbian forces, to the best of your knowledge? And I appreciate that you were not necessarily at the front lines for that entire eight-day period.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I stayed in Nishor for seven days and then I went to Bellanice because that was continuous. I don't know when they withdrew, but I know this, that there was shelling every day in Nishor. We stayed in the basements because there were -- there was nowhere else to go. And then we went to Bellanice after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, just so that there's no confusion, ma'am, is it your testimony that the battles between the KLA and the Serbian forces occurred constantly on a daily basis for the entire week that you were in Nishor?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: There was shelling every day in Nishor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about the activities of your -- pardon me, of the KLA fighters, was that every day as well?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know that. I did not see the KLA. I don't know whether the fight -- they were fighting the KLA or just shelling the village where we were. I couldn't tell you. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In any event, the Serbian force --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Mrs. Fondaj, in your statement you say the following words: "Because of the resistance of the KLA from the village of Semetisht where they were deployed, the Serb army was not able to enter Nishor."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now you've told us that you did not see the KLA, you don't know whether they were fighting. What is the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the army was there. Whether they were fighting regularly, every day, or how they were fighting, I don't know. I can tell you about the shelling in Nishor, but I know this, that the KLA was for seven days in Semetisht. Seven or eight days we were in Nishor, there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I gather from your testimony here today it sounds like there was additional fighting for another three days while you -- when you left Nishor and were in Belanica. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We went to Bellanice. I don't know whether there was any fighting. I was in Bellanice from the 28th to the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now when you went to Belanica, during the time-period that you were in Belanica, did you see any KLA members either in Belanica or passing through Belanica during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I did not see any. I was inside the house. I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you did not leave the house. Now, let me focus on the date I believe you stated that the Serb forces entered the village, April the 1st. And I want to ask you to be as precise as possible. In your statement you state that they came into the village between 1300 and 1400 hours. Can you confirm that or be more precise or just let us know whether that time is accurate?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: That time is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you talk about -- you talk today about the night you spent with others in Belanica waiting to leave that village after the Serb forces came. And I want to ask you about something else that you mention in your statement. In your statement you mention that during that evening you could see flames of the NATO bombs when they hit targets in the surrounding area. Now, I want to ask you first of all: Did you see that with your own eyes, the flames?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them with my own eyes, the flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We could see the burst of flame, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And approximately how many NATO attacks are we talking about that you witnessed? Was it a single event? Was it multiple attacks that evening?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Only one. It was about 3.00 in the morning, 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning. There was this big fire. The flames lit the sky, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell approximately how close to your position was the target that had been struck by these NATO attacks?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know how close it was. There was -- the sky was lit by the flames, but I couldn't tell you where exactly that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did that NATO strike cause fear amongst the persons in Belanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, it did not cause any fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you then about what I believe you testified to happening that next morning. You stated that some individuals had come up to your tractor and first asked for money from the inhabitants of the tractors, and in your -- in your statement you describe these individuals as Serb police officers. But today you described a variety of different uniforms. And I'd like to ask you specifically about the 20 persons that came up to your tractor, what type of uniform did they have on? Could you describe that uniform for me.

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Those who came to our tractor had masks on. Only one of them did not wear a mask. The others were masked, painted, had bandannas, knives, brandishing knives around the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see any type of insignia on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you see any type of badges on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. Well, I wasn't in fact paying too much attention to these insignia, but I know that they were masked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you weren't paying too much attention to these individuals, how is it then that you are -- able to identify them as being Serb police officers?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I did not say they were officers. They were wearing all kinds of uniforms. I don't know who of them was the officer. I never joined the army or was in the army, so I don't know these things. But there were policemen because they had the letters "police" which I could see. But the other insignia that you're asking, the other signs, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did these men that came up to your tractor to ask for money, did they have the insignia that you have described with the letters "police"?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: There were policemen there, but those who came to my tractor were masked. There were policemen everywhere, but the ones who came to my tractor were masked. Just one of them did not wear a mask, and they asked for money. They went from tractor to tractor, as I explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you I believe stated that some persons that came up were in fact naked. Is that accurate or was that something that came through the translation wrong?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: They were naked from the waist up and were painted, had bandannas and knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the weather like that day? Wasn't it fairly cold?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: It was April. I don't know whether they felt cold or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me just check the transcript for a second. I think I have to ask one more question before we leave Belanica. I wanted to ask you to -- to clear up your answer when I asked you whether the persons who came up to the tractor, whether they had the letters "police" written on their uniform. Could you just answer that, did they or did they not? You've already mentioned that they had masks, so we know all that. I'm asking about the uniforms. Did you see this insignia that you have described with the letters "police" on the uniforms of the individuals you've described?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see -- I couldn't see properly. I was scared. I saw that they were wearing masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. Now I think I'd like to move on and just ask you a few questions relating to when you arrived at the border. Now, when you came to the border you said that the border police were very nice to you and assured you -- and when assured that you had all your identity documents in your possession they let you across the border. What kind of uniform did these individuals wear?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: They were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And -- I don't know if my mic's working. And with respect to these individuals, did they have the insignia on their uniforms that spelled "police"?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, on their backs, yes, big letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And while you were present at the border, you did not personally see anyone's identification cards being confiscated, did you?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. They did not take any from our tractor. It was 2.00 in the morning, it was night, the driver went up to them and told: We are okay, so they said: You can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now in your statement I believe you just mentioned that there was an incident that you heard about some two hours later regarding other persons at the border post. And I want to -- they had a problem. And I want to confirm with you that you were still not at the border when this happened, were you, that is to say you did not eye-witness that interaction?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: We saw these things. After we crossed the border to Albania, we were given food and helped, and the next tractor that came after us, they were beaten up. Even the elderly were beaten up. That's where I saw them. Because we were waiting at the border inside the Albanian territory. We were being helped there, assisted before we went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it was still dark outside at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it was about 3.00 in the morning. At 2.00, we were at the border and then for one hour we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour, if I could just consult my notes, I think I'm close to concluding my part of this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Zed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Fondaj. My name is Nadia Zed, and along with Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Aleksic I'm representing General Pavkovic, and I just have a few very, very brief questions for you this morning. Just to start off with, you've already talked about this eight days of fighting between the Serb forces and the KLA, and in your statement you indicate that after the eight days of fighting the KLA had to withdraw to a mountain above Belanica. And I take it that that mountain is very -- is very near the village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know where they went. We were in Bellanice. We didn't have KLA in Bellanice. They fought, but where they fought I don't know. I was in Nishor for seven days. There was shelling going on every day. The KLA was in Semetisht. As for this mountain above Bellanice, I don't know, because I've never been to that part, and I don't know the villages in that part in the mountains there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Fondaj, in your statement it says: "After eight days of fighting, the KLA had to withdraw to a mountain above Bellanice." Did you say that to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did, in my statement. But I don't know exactly in which mountain. It was a mountain, but I don't know exactly where they went. And we didn't see them. We just heard that the KLA had -- withdrew because all these forces had come to Bellanice. There was no longer KLA there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Zed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: You also indicated in your statement that you were aware that the Serb forces would come to Belanica. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Well, we heard on the radio that the villages around Prizren, Krushevo, Krusha e Madhe, and so forth were already expelled and people made to go to Albania, and we were anticipating this. We knew that this was going to happen to us as well. That's why I said so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Okay. Did you also think that the Serb forces, if they were looking for the KLA and they were in the area of Belanica, in the mountain, that perhaps that would draw the Serb forces to Belanica?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No. As they expelled the others before us, the Serb forces expelled us. It was our turn. There was no KLA there. We were gathered there. In order for us not to go to the mountains, we gathered in those large numbers in Bellanice. And then they came and they told us to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Fondaj, in your statement you indicated that on April 2nd, when you were preparing to leave, you were in a bad mood and at that moment you blamed your husband for being in this situation. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I blamed my husband at the moment when they pointed their automatic rifle at me. And since he used to be a policeman, I thought that they know him and that's why they could massacre my children. And another reason why I blamed him was because he wasn't around with me and with my children during those difficult times.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Ms. Fondaj, did you ever return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, in July. I don't know the date exactly, but it was July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Okay. And just to conclude, in the last paragraph of your statement it says: "We fled Kosovo because of Serb threats and not because of NATO bombing." Mr. Ekdahl, the man who took your statement back in June of 2001, put that in your statement and told you that it was important, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that it was important to say that. I said that myself, that we left because of the Serb forces and not because of NATO. I said it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Those are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, in your evidence you stated while you were in Nishor, that week the village was being shelled. Was there any outgoing fire from Nishor towards Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: No, not from the village of Nishor towards the Serb positions. It was only the population in Nishor, from my village and the surrounding villages, I didn't see any KLA in Nishor. But they said that they had seen KLA in Semetisht.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mrs. Fondaj, you say that the KLA was holding up resistance in Semetisht. How far is the village of Semetisht from Nishor, just approximately?

utterances.speaker: HAMIDE FONDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe 5 or 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Those are all my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fondaj, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Kravetz, who is the next witness? Sorry, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be Shyrete Berisha, and we will do a little re-shuffle here on the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness is brought in, I would like to object to the admission of Mr. Fondaj's statement. I believe that if the Defence wants to introduce this statement as an exhibit, they should call the witness who gave the statement for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can respond. First of all, I think the objection is untimely. I believe they're talking about Mr. Fondaj's statement -- oh, it's been corrected.
